title: Graph Neural Networks Are Not Continuous Across Graph Resolutions
claim: The same underlying object can be represented at fine and coarse resolutions, yielding very different graph structures that a model should treat consistently.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, fine graph beside coarse-grained graph, labeled (a)/(b)
description: Two side-by-side panels show the same molecule, ethane, as graphs at two resolutions. Panel (a) on the left is the original graph. It has two central magenta nodes (carbon) joined by a horizontal edge. Each carbon connects to three green nodes (hydrogen), so there are six green leaves in total. Two leaves point up and down from each carbon, and one points outward to the left or right. Panel (b) on the right is the coarse-grained graph. It has just two orange super-nodes joined by a single edge. The nodes use soft gradient shading, and the edges are thin blue lines on a white background. Large serif labels (a) and (b) sit at the bottom corners. The eye goes first to the larger, branching graph on the left, then to the much simpler orange pair on the right.
caption: (a) Original graph G corresponding to the Ethane molecule with Carbon in purple and Hydrogen in green (b) Coarse grained G with aggregate Carbon-Hydrogen super-nodes in orange
abstract: We show that contrary to conventional wisdom in the community, graph neural networks (GNNs) are not continuous with respect to all natural modes of graph convergence. As a result, GNNs may generate substantially different latent representations for graphs that are very similar. In particular they assign vastly different latent embeddings to graphs that represent the same underlying object at different resolution scales. We trace this failure of continuity back to a structural obstruction arising from commonly used information-propagation schemes. Building on this insight we then derive a principled modification to standard GNN architectures which equips models with continuity across scales. The proposed modification enables consistent integration of distinct resolutions and reliable generalization between them. We systematically validate our theoretical findings in a wide range of numerical experiments.
